prompt: What does Lambda's concurrency count?
hint: Think of what one execution environment is doing at a given instant.

choices.text: The requests that arrive in one second, however long each takes
choices.why: That is the request rate. Concurrency also depends on how long each request runs.

choices.text: The threads one environment runs side by side to serve its requests
choices.why: That is a web server's model. A Lambda environment serves one request at a time.

choices.text: The requests in flight right now, one environment each
choices.why: Right. Each request holds an environment for as long as it runs, and concurrency is how many are held.

choices.text: The functions deployed in the account in that Region
choices.why: The number of functions says nothing about how many requests are running.

prompt: A function receives 200 requests a second and each runs for 0.25 s. How many execution environments are busy at once, by Little's law?
hint: Requests per second times seconds per request.

prompt: A function handles 80 requests a second at 0.15 s each. Its database slows down and every request now takes 1.5 s, at the same traffic. What is its concurrency now?
hint: Only one of the two factors changed.

prompt: Two simultaneous calls to the emulator both fail, and its log says ReserveFailed: AlreadyReserved. What does that show about Lambda on AWS?
hint: The emulator is one environment. What would AWS do with the second request?

choices.text: That Lambda refuses a second request arriving while the first still runs
choices.why: That is the emulator's limitation read as Lambda's. On AWS the second request gets a second environment.

choices.text: That the Python handler is not thread-safe
choices.why: The handler never ran twice. The refusal came from the emulator, before any code.

choices.text: That one environment holds one request; Lambda would start a second
choices.why: Right. The emulator has no second environment to start, which is exactly what Lambda does instead.

choices.text: That the port Docker published accepts one connection at a time, which is a limit of Docker and not of Lambda
choices.why: A published port accepts many connections. The log line is the emulator reserving its environment.

prompt: By Little's law, the requests in flight equal the arrival rate multiplied by the ___ of each request.
hint: How long it lasts.

prompt: What is the default concurrency limit of an AWS account for Lambda?
hint: It is a pool, and it is shared.

choices.text: 1,000 concurrent executions for each function, in every Region
choices.why: The thousand is not per function: every function in the Region draws on the same pool.

choices.text: 1,000 requests a second for the account
choices.why: That mixes the rate with concurrency. The pool counts requests in flight, and the rate allowed is ten times it.

choices.text: None, because Lambda bills each environment it starts
choices.why: Lambda does bill per use, and it also has a limit; the limit is what keeps a mistake small.

choices.text: 1,000 concurrent executions per Region, shared by all the account's functions
choices.why: Right. One pool per account and Region, and a quota that Service Quotas can raise.

prompt: Match each way a function was invoked to what a throttle does to the request.
hint: Who called, and does anybody hold the request?

pairs.right: The caller receives a 429 at once
Lambda retries it from its internal queue for up to six hours
The message stays in the queue and returns after its visibility timeout
The shard waits behind the retried batch

right_distractors: The request waits in a line behind the busy environments

prompt: A function runs for 4 ms and receives 15,000 requests a second, in an account with the default quota of 1,000 and nothing else running. What happens?
hint: Work out the concurrency, then remember the second limit.

choices.text: Part of the traffic is throttled: the rate allowed is 10,000/s, and only 60 environments are busy
choices.why: Right. 15,000 × 0.004 = 60 in flight is far below 1,000, but the rate allowed is ten times the quota.

choices.text: Every request succeeds, because 60 environments are well inside the pool
choices.why: The concurrency is right and the conclusion is not: Lambda also limits requests per second.

choices.text: Every request above 1,000 a second is throttled, because the quota is 1,000
choices.why: That reads the quota as a rate. It counts requests in flight, and the rate allowed is 10,000 a second.

choices.text: Lambda queues what is over the limit and serves it a second later
choices.why: Lambda does not queue a synchronous request; a throttle is an error returned to the caller.

prompt: Which of these are true of the account's concurrency limit? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about who shares it and who enforces it.

choices.text: It is shared by every function in the account and Region
choices.why: Right. One pool per account and Region.

choices.text: A load test on one function can throttle the others
choices.why: Right. They draw on the same thousand.

choices.text: moto enforces it, so a script tested there shows where it bites
choices.why: moto keeps no count of anything running and throttles nothing.

choices.text: It is a quota that a request through Service Quotas raises
choices.why: Right. It is a quota, not a wall.

choices.text: It counts requests per second rather than requests in flight
choices.why: It counts requests in flight; the rate is a separate limit of ten times the quota.

prompt: An S3 notification invokes a function asynchronously and is throttled. What happens to the event?
hint: Who is holding the event once S3 has handed it over?

choices.text: S3 receives the 429 and sends the notification again later
choices.why: S3 handed the event to Lambda and is out of the picture; the retries are Lambda's.

choices.text: It is dropped at once
choices.why: It is kept and retried first. It is dropped only after the maximum age, and only if no destination is set.

choices.text: Lambda holds it and retries for up to six hours, then uses the on-failure destination
choices.why: Right. The asynchronous path absorbs a throttle quietly, which is why it can look like slowness.

choices.text: It is moved into an SQS queue that S3 keeps for the bucket, and waits there until there is room
choices.why: S3 keeps no queue for a bucket; the internal queue that holds the event belongs to Lambda.

prompt: What does a reserved concurrency of 100 do for a function?
hint: It is the same number seen from two sides.

choices.text: Starts 100 environments in advance and bills them by the second
choices.why: That is provisioned concurrency. A reservation starts nothing and costs nothing.

choices.text: Guarantees it 100, and lets it borrow from the unreserved pool above that
choices.why: The reservation is also a ceiling: the 101st concurrent request is throttled.

choices.text: Guarantees it 100 and caps it at 100, at no charge
choices.why: Right. A floor and a ceiling at once, and one number on the function.

choices.text: Caps it at 100 but does not protect it from the other functions
choices.why: It does protect it: no other function can use the 100 reserved for it.

prompt: An account has the default pool of 1,000. checkout reserves 300 and orders reserves 250. What is the most a third function can reserve?
hint: AWS keeps a floor of 100 unreserved.

prompt: A function writes to a database that accepts 100 connections, and each environment holds one. A spike would start 300 environments. Which setting protects the database?
hint: Which setting is a ceiling?

choices.text: A provisioned concurrency of 100
choices.why: Provisioned concurrency is not a cap: requests above it are served by on-demand environments, which open more connections.

choices.text: A request to raise the account's limit, so that the throttles stop
choices.why: A larger pool lets more environments reach the database, which is the problem.

choices.text: A reserved concurrency below 100 on that function, such as 80
choices.why: Right. The 81st request is throttled before it reaches the database, and nothing is half done.

choices.text: A reserved concurrency of 0 on every other function in the account
choices.why: That stops every other function and leaves this one free to start 300 environments.

prompt: Put the steps of giving a new function a reservation against moto in the order they have to happen.
hint: Each step needs what the one before it made.
items: Create the role with a trust policy for lambda.amazonaws.com
Run create-function, naming the role and the zip
trap: Zipping before creating the role also works; the role and the package both have to exist before create-function names them.

prompt: moto accepted a reserved concurrency of 2000 on a function. What does that tell you?
hint: What does moto check, and what does it leave to AWS?

choices.text: That AWS allows a reservation above the pool when nothing else is running
choices.why: AWS refuses any reservation that leaves less than 100 unreserved, busy or not.

choices.text: That moto's account has a pool larger than the default
choices.why: moto has no pool at all; it stores the number without comparing it with anything.

choices.text: That the floor of 100 applies to accounts with several functions
choices.why: The floor applies to every account. moto simply does not model it.

choices.text: Only that the call is well formed; AWS would refuse the number
choices.why: Right. moto answers like AWS and enforces much less, so a success here proves the shape of the call and nothing more.

prompt: Where is provisioned concurrency configured?
hint: What Lambda keeps ready has to be code that cannot change under it.

choices.text: On $LATEST, so that it follows every update of the code
choices.why: AWS refuses $LATEST, because it is the editable copy and can change under the ready environments.

choices.text: On a version, or on an alias that points at one
choices.why: Right. An alias is the usual choice, because a deployment moves it and the environments follow.

choices.text: On the function as a whole, the way reserved concurrency is
choices.why: A reservation is on the function; provisioned concurrency is on a qualifier, a version or an alias.

choices.text: On the account, where every function in the Region shares it
choices.why: There is no account-wide provisioned pool; it is set per version or alias and drawn from the concurrency pool.

prompt: Four environments of 0.5 GB are kept ready for a month of 730 hours in sa-east-1, at 0.0000066372 USD per GB-second. What does keeping them ready cost, before a single request, in USD to the cent?
hint: Environments × GB × seconds × price; 730 hours is 2,628,000 seconds.

prompt: A function has 10 provisioned environments and 25 requests arrive at once. What happens to the other 15?
hint: Provisioned concurrency is not a cap.

choices.text: They are throttled with a 429, because 10 is the limit
choices.why: That treats provisioned as a ceiling. Only a reservation caps a function.

choices.text: They are served by on-demand environments, each with a cold start
choices.why: Right. Beyond the provisioned number Lambda starts ordinary environments, if the pool allows.

choices.text: They wait in a line until one of the ten provisioned environments is free
choices.why: Lambda does not queue a request behind a busy environment; it starts another.

choices.text: Lambda adds 15 provisioned environments and bills them from that moment
choices.why: The provisioned number changes only when you, or a scaling policy, change it.

prompt: A team in sa-east-1 wants provisioned concurrency on a function that is busy 90% of the time, to save money. Using the sheet of 16 October 2026, are they right?
hint: Compare what provisioned saves per GB-second of running with what it charges per GB-second kept ready.

choices.text: Yes: articles put the break-even near 60% use, and 90% is above it
choices.why: That figure is arithmetic on another Region's prices. On São Paulo's sheet there is no break-even.

choices.text: Yes, but only above 95% use, where the discount on running catches up
choices.why: The break-even works out at 562%, which no month reaches.

choices.text: No: saving 0.0000011800 per GB-second run never repays 0.0000066372 per GB-second kept
choices.why: Right. In sa-east-1 provisioned concurrency is bought for latency, at any level of use.

choices.text: It makes no difference, because requests are billed the same on both
choices.why: Requests do cancel out, and duration does not: provisioned adds a charge for every second kept ready.

prompt: Put these functions in order of concurrency, the smallest first.
hint: Multiply each rate by its duration.
trap: The busiest function by requests a second is the least concurrent: 500 × 0.02 = 10.

prompt: Match each setting to what it is.
hint: Which ones cost money, and which ones only draw a line?

pairs.right: A free floor and ceiling for one function
Environments initialised in advance, billed by the second
The pool every function in the Region draws on
The 100 AWS keeps for functions without a reservation

right_distractors: A line that holds requests until an environment is free

prompt: Which of these did moto 5.2.3 do in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them it did; the others it refused, ignored or does not have.

choices.text: Stored a reserved concurrency on a function
choices.why: Right. put-function-concurrency and get-function both answered.

choices.text: Refused a reservation larger than the pool
choices.why: It accepted 2000 without comparing it with anything.

choices.text: Published a version and created an alias pointing at it
choices.why: Right. publish-version and create-alias both work in moto.

choices.text: Configured ten provisioned environments behind an alias
choices.why: PutProvisionedConcurrencyConfig answered with a 404 page: moto has not implemented it.

choices.text: Printed the account's limits with get-account-settings
choices.why: That operation is missing from moto too, and returned the same 404 page.

prompt: What does a reserved concurrency of 0 do?
hint: It is a ceiling as well as a floor.

choices.text: Removes the reservation and returns the function to the shared pool
choices.why: That is delete-function-concurrency. A reservation of 0 is a ceiling of zero.

choices.text: Throttles every request: the function stops, and is not deleted
choices.why: Right. It is the switch for an incident or a function calling itself in a loop.

choices.text: Lets the function use the whole unreserved pool
choices.why: That is a function with no reservation at all; 0 is a reservation, and the smallest one.

choices.text: Nothing, because AWS refuses a reservation smaller than 1
choices.why: AWS accepts 0, and documents it as the way to stop a function's invocations.

prompt: On demand in sa-east-1, duration is 0.0000166667 USD per GB-second. A 512 MB function serves 3,000,000 requests of 200 ms each in a month. What is its duration charge, in USD to the cent?
hint: 512 MB is 0.5 GB; GB × seconds × requests × price.
